cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: What three transactions does LOCATIO CONDUCTIO cover?
cards.back:
One contract type covering lease, contract for work and contract of employment.
• LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI: a thing made available for use (and fruits) against payment.
• LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS: paid production of a defined result (OPUS).
• LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERARUM: paid use of someone's labour (OPERAE).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: What are the key features of LOCATIO CONDUCTIO as a contract?
cards.back:
Synallagmatic, consensual contract; the counter-performance (rent, fee, wage) is the MERCES.
• Concluded by agreement on the use or services and on the MERCES.
• MERCES as a rule: money, seriously intended, determined (MERCES CERTA).
• MERCES CERTA: Gai Inst 3.142–143 (Case 144).
• Actions: ACTIO LOCATI and ACTIO CONDUCTI — both BONAE FIDEI IUDICIA.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO vs COMMODATUM vs MANDATUM — what is the decisive difference?
cards.back:
Payment: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO needs a MERCES; free use of a thing is COMMODATUM, free services are MANDATUM.
• Synallagmatic deals fitting neither LOCATIO nor sale = innominate contracts (Gai Inst 3.144, Case 144).
• Rent NUMMO UNO (one coin) is void, not seriously meant — Ulpian D 41.2.10.2 (Case 146).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: Who is LOCATOR and who is CONDUCTOR in each type of LOCATIO CONDUCTIO?
cards.back:
LOCATOR = the party who puts something at the other's disposal; he sues by ACTIO LOCATI, the CONDUCTOR by ACTIO CONDUCTI.
• Lease: lessor = LOCATOR (the thing); lessee = CONDUCTOR.
• Work: customer = LOCATOR (often the materials); contractor = CONDUCTOR.
• Employment: employee = LOCATOR (his time and labour); employer = CONDUCTOR.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: Continuous vs non-recurring obligation — how do the three types of LOCATIO CONDUCTIO differ?
cards.back:
Lease and employment are continuous obligations; the contract for work creates a non-recurring obligation.
• Continuous obligations run for a fixed or an unlimited term.
• Roman law knew only fixed-term employment contracts.
• Like sale, a synallagmatic BONA FIDES contract: PRETIUM CERTUM rules apply, adapted, to MERCES CERTA.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: What is LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI and what can be its object?
cards.back:
Agreement granting use (and, where applicable, the fruits) of a thing against remuneration.
• Objects: chiefly material, non-consumable things, but also rights (e.g. lease of a usufruct).
• Modern theory: usufructuary lease (fruits) vs lease (use only); Roman jurists drew no such distinction.
• ABGB umbrella term: "Bestandvertrag" (§§ 1090–1121 ABGB).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: What are the lessor's (LOCATOR's) duties and risks in LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI?
cards.back:
Place the thing at the lessee's disposal and keep it usable as agreed, including repairs.
• As owner he bears the risk of damage, loss or destruction by VIS MAIOR.
• He also bears the rent risk: no or reduced rent after VIS MAIOR.
• Probably reimburses necessary or useful expenses (Scaevola D 19.2.61 pr, Case 159).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: What are the lessee's (CONDUCTOR's) duties in LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI?
cards.back:
Pay rent for the use and, from taking over the thing, answer for CUSTODIA.
• Liable for harm through DOLUS, CULPA or lack of proper guarding.
• Usufructuary lease of a farm: duty to cultivate properly (Paulus D 19.2.54.1, Case 160).
• IUS TOLLENDI: may remove additions he built (Ulpian D 19.2.19.4).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: Property link: the lessee as detentor — what kind of possession does he have, and why does it matter?
cards.back:
The lessee is a mere detentor (NATURALIS POSSESSIO): he holds for the lessor, who keeps mediate proprietary possession.
• Detentor = holds with ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI; tenants and lessees are the textbook examples.
• Lease is a contract IN PERSONAM — the lessee gets no right in rem.
• Usufructuary lessee (COLONUS) acquires fruits only by PERCEPTIO, derivatively from the lessor.
• If the lessee buys the thing: TRADITIO BREVI MANU, no handback needed.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: Property link: the landlord's tacit lien — what is the PIGNUS TACITUM in lease?
cards.back:
A pledge arising automatically on conclusion of the lease, without express agreement.
• Lessor of a flat: lien over the tenant's INVECTA ILLATA (movables brought in to stay).
• Lessor of farmland: PIGNUS in the fruits of the land.
• Landlord may seize by self-help; tenant reclaims impounded things by INTERDICTUM DE MIGRANDO.
• Default rule (IUS DISPOSITIVUM): the parties may exclude it.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: types and lease (REI)
cards.front: Ordinary termination vs termination for good reason — when does each end a lease?
cards.back:
Ordinary termination ends an open-ended lease; termination for good reason ends any lease EX NUNC.
• Ordinary: unilateral right of every party; no need to show continuation is unreasonable.
• LEX CONTRACTUS often fixes dates and notice periods; BONA FIDES bars untimely termination.
• Good reason: fixed-term or permanent lease, when continuing is unreasonable for one party.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: The lessee damages the leased thing by fault or lack of CUSTODIA — what does the lessor get?
cards.back:
Damages and, in principle, the rent too — the lessee cannot escape rent through damage he caused.
• Cf Alfenus D 19.2.29 (Case 162) and D 19.2.30.4 (Case 161).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 163 (Ulpian/Labeo D 19.2.13.7), variants 1–2: tenant A flees approaching soldiers without informing B, or without resisting. Is A liable?
cards.back:
Yes — in both variants A is liable on the lease for harm caused by his culpable omissions.
• Harm: looted windows and other items.
• Rent, variant 1 (no notice): possibly ends, like loss without fault.
• Rent, variant 2 (no reasonable resistance): fault — he probably still owes rent.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 163, variant 3: tenant A leaves before the soldiers arrive, with no way to inform B or to resist. Result?
cards.back:
A is not liable: an attack by armed troops is VIS MAIOR, whose risk the owner B bears.
• A cannot be expected to continue the lease — it ends.
• Neither party has further contractual claims against the other.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: VIS MAIOR damages the leased thing — who bears the risk, and what can the lessee claim?
cards.back:
The lessor (CASUM SENTIT DOMINUS if he is owner); the defective performance gives the lessee warranty remedies.
• Remedies: rent reduction (REMISSIO MERCEDIS) or rescission.
• New building cuts off light → reduction, even termination (Gaius D 19.2.25.2, Case 148).
• Demolition seriously curtailing use → deduct rent; minor inconvenience → nothing (Alfenus D 19.2.27 pr, Case 149).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Warranty in lease vs warranty in sale — from when do the remedies operate?
cards.back:
Lease remedies operate only EX NUNC, from when performance became defective; sale remedies operate retroactively (EX TUNC).
• So full rent is owed for the period before the impairment.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 151 (Servius in Ulpian D 19.2.15.2): which harms to a leased field reduce the rent, and which do not?
cards.back:
VIS MAIOR from outside → no or reduced rent; VITIA QUAE EX IPSA RE ORIUNTUR → lessee's loss, full rent.
• VIS MAIOR = VIS CUI RESISTI NON POTEST: birds, enemy invasion, mudslide, fungus or heat, earthquake.
• Defects from the thing itself: wine turning sour, seed ruined by worms or weeds.
• Rationale: production risks tied to the lessee's activity fall in his sphere.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: What is COLONIA PARTIARIA, and how does it relate to REMISSIO MERCEDIS?
cards.back:
Sharecropping: the COLONUS PARTIARIUS pays a fixed share of the crop instead of money rent.
• Permanent sharing of crop-failure risk (Gaius D 19.2.25.6, Case 153).
• REMISSIO MERCEDIS = rent reduction after VIS MAIOR.
• Parallel: in both the lessor shares in a bad harvest.
• Exception to the rule that MERCES must be money.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 150 (Alfenus/Paulus D 19.2.30 pr): A lets a house to B for 30; B sublets flats for 40. A demolishes the house. What can B claim?
cards.back:
Unsound house: B reclaims rent beyond his use until demolition; demolition without good reason: also his lost sub-lease income.
• A culpable (or knowing) lessor is liable for consequential losses.
• Here: B getting less from X and Y than the agreed 40.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 154 (Ulpian D 19.2.19.1), part 1: A unknowingly lets leaky barrels to B; wine leaks out and causes damage. Is A liable?
cards.back:
Yes — Cassius: ignorance does not release the lessor; A must compensate B's interest.
• Assessed like a sale of leaky vessels (Pomponius D 19.1.6.4, Case 114).
• Very likely includes consequential damage: spoilt wine, damaged floor.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 154, part 2: A lets pastures where poisonous plants grow; B's cattle sicken or die. Does A's knowledge matter?
cards.back:
Yes: unaware, A gets no rent (like rescission); aware, A is liable for B's interest.
• Interest probably covers all losses directly from the defect.
• E.g. the animals' loss of value and vet fees.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: What does "sale breaks lease" mean, and why is the phrase misleading?
cards.back:
The buyer, as new owner, may expel the lessee, who then has eviction claims against the lessor (Gaius D 19.2.25.1, Case 158).
• The buyer owes the lessee nothing contractually.
• Not the sale but the eviction "breaks" it; the lease is not terminated.
• Lessor's performance becomes defective → lessee claims expectation interest.
• Lessor may offer a comparable flat instead (Ulpian/Pomponius D 19.2.9 pr, Case 155).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Ulpian D 45.1.38.17: ALTERI STIPULARI NEMO POTEST — what does it mean for a lessee whose landlord sells?
cards.back:
No one can stipulate for a third party: Roman law knows no true contracts for the benefit of third parties.
• True contract: A and B contract so that C can claim performance.
• Claimless third party: performance to C agreed, without an enforceable claim.
• Buyer promises seller not to evict: lessee cannot sue; evicting buyer is liable to the seller.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: lease — risk, defects, eviction
cards.front: Case 156 (Ulpian D 19.2.7, Tryphoninus D 19.2.8): A lets to B for 50; B sublets to C for 60; owner X evicts C. What can B claim from A?
cards.back:
His interest via ACTIO CONDUCTI — essentially what he owes C, which may exceed the 50 he paid A.
• C's expectation interest may exceed 60, e.g. a comparable flat costs 80.
• B prepaid A 50 and pays C 80 → B claims 80 from A.
• B has not yet paid A → B claims 30 (80 minus 50).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: What is LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS?
cards.back:
A contract to produce an OPUS (work, result) for remuneration.
• OPUS ranges from a musical performance or heavy transport to teaching or building a house.
• Contractor (CONDUCTOR) must deliver the result; customer (LOCATOR) pays the fee.
• Non-recurring obligation.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: What is the contractor's standard of liability for the customer's things?
cards.back:
DOLUS, CULPA and CUSTODIA, insofar as he holds the customer's things.
• IMPERITIA (lack of skill) counts as negligence — he acts as an expert (Ulpian/Celsus D 19.2.9.5, Case 165).
• FULLO: coat gnawed by mice in storage, or wrong coat returned → breach (Ulpian D 19.2.13.6, Case 166).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Example 61: Phobos gives washerwoman Helena his coat to clean within a week. Who keeps the fee if it stays uncleaned?
cards.back:
Depends on whose sphere caused the failure: Phobos demands it back next day → Helena keeps the fee; Helena falls ill → she loses it.
• Fee owed if the OPUS fails for reasons outside the contractor's sphere.
• Not owed if failure lies in the contractor's sphere or fault.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: What is ADPROBATIO in the contract for work, and what are its effects?
cards.back:
The customer's acceptance of the offered work — comparable to TRADITIO in sale; on acceptance the contract is fulfilled.
• From ADPROBATIO the work is in the customer's risk sphere.
• Later defects: warranty rules apply.
• Before payment the contractor has a right of retention over the customer's things.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Contract for work and materials: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO or EMPTIO VENDITIO? (Example 62)
cards.back:
Contractor uses (mainly) his own materials → classically a sub-type of sale; initially disputed.
• Thetis supplies cloth to tailor Philemon → LOCATIO CONDUCTIO; picks his cloth → EMPTIO VENDITIO.
• Pomponius (Sabinus) D 18.1.20 (Case 63); Gai Inst 3.147 (Case 144).
• Building contract: always LOCATIO CONDUCTIO — the land, the principal thing, is the customer's.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Property link: the customer supplies materials for a contract for work — does the contractor become owner by SPECIFICATIO?
cards.back:
No — both agree the materials are worked on for the customer, who stays owner; the contractor is a mere detentor.
• SPECIFICATIO = making a NOVA SPECIES; MEDIA SENTENTIA gives irreversible products to the maker.
• That rule does not apply to transformation by mutual consent (LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS).
• Exception: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO IRREGULARIS — the contractor becomes owner of the material.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 169 (Ulpian D 19.2.13.3): a slave left with a contractor for training is taken abroad and captured or dies. Is the contractor liable?
cards.back:
Yes — culpable breach: capture or death is VIS MAIOR, but the contractor's breach made it possible.
• Not liable if the training contract allowed taking the slave abroad.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 170 (Gaius D 19.2.25.7): a column breaks while A is transporting it for B. Is A liable?
cards.back:
Yes, for his own and his helpers' culpable conduct, measured against a DILIGENTISSIMUS.
• DILIGENTISSIMUS = an exceptionally careful man.
• Hidden flaw in the stone despite careful handling → not liable.
• Fee presumably owed so far as he performed (column delivered, gate damaged unloading).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 165a (Gai Inst 3.205): the customer's thing is stolen from the contractor. Who has the ACTIO FURTI?
cards.back:
The contractor, since he bears the theft loss through CUSTODIA liability; if he is insolvent, the customer as owner keeps it.
• Same interplay for the commodatary (Modestinus Coll 10.2.6, Case 28).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: What is the RECEPTUM liability of NAUTAE, CAUPONES and STABULARII?
cards.back:
Guarantee that guests' or passengers' belongings are not stolen or damaged, enforced by ACTIO DE RECEPTO.
• Strict: compensation does not depend on fault.
• VIS MAIOR excluded via EXCEPTIO DOLI → scope equals CUSTODIA.
• Justified by these trades' exceptional dishonesty (Ulpian D 4.9.3.1).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: How did RECEPTUM liability develop, and does it presuppose a LOCATIO CONDUCTIO?
cards.back:
From express promises (SALVAM FORE) to an objective duty arising from mere handover (RECIPERE).
• No LOCATIO needed: also gratuitous carriage or lodging (Paulus D 4.9.6 pr, Case 215).
• Covers freight and personal belongings (Ulpian D 4.9.1.6, Case 214); interest suffices, not ownership.
• Modern: §§ 970 ff ABGB — "danger of the open house".

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 168 (Labeo/Paulus D 14.2.10 pr): A ships B's slaves for a fee; one dies on board. Is full freight owed?
cards.back:
Paulus (prevailing view): yes — PERICULUM EST LOCATORIS once the slave was taken on board.
• Natural death = VIS MAIOR; the owner bears the loss of the slave itself.
• Labeo: no freight for the dead slave.
• Parties may agree otherwise, e.g. payment only on disembarkation.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 167 (Labeo/Paulus D 19.2.62): a canal's embankment collapses after completion but before ADPROBATIO. Is the fee owed?
cards.back:
Paulus asks whose sphere caused it: VITIUM OPERIS → contractor gets nothing; VITIUM SOLI → customer pays.
• VITIUM OPERIS = faulty workmanship; VITIUM SOLI = soil unsuitable for a canal.
• Labeo, without a sphere test: contractor bears payment risk, gets nothing.
• Cf § 1168 ABGB (comparable sphere distinction).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Theory of spheres: how is the payment risk allocated in LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS?
cards.back:
Contractor bears payment risk only for (culpable) defects in his production process; otherwise PERICULUM EST LOCATORIS.
• Includes VIS MAIOR not clearly attributable to either sphere.
• Parallel in lease: VIS MAIOR vs VITIA EX IPSA RE (Case 151).
• Parallel in employment: wage risk also decided by sphere.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Case 167a (Javolenus D 19.2.51.1): work paid in daily instalments, quality to be proved by ADPROBATIO, is done faultily. Result?
cards.back:
Contractor liable; the customer sues by ACTIO LOCATI — the payment mode does not change liability.
• Customer refuses ADPROBATIO → contractor in debtor's delay.
• Or approves, then claims price reduction or rescission.
• If the customer dictated the technical execution, defects are not the contractor's.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: What makes LOCATIO CONDUCTIO IRREGULARIS "irregular"?
cards.back:
The contractor becomes owner of the material on handover, instead of a mere detentor.
• Precious metal for vessels or rings: may use it or his own; must transfer the finished work.
• Mixed grain of several owners in a ship's hold (Alfenus/Paulus D 19.2.31, Case 172).
• Reason: practical advantages for his performance.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: contract for work (OPERIS)
cards.front: Property link: grain of several owners poured together into a ship's hold (Case 172) — who owns it?
cards.back:
The carrier becomes sole owner; the charterers do not become co-owners.
• Normal COMMIXTIO: each keeps his share (VINDICATIO PRO PARTE), or co-ownership if mixed by consent.
• Each delivery to a recipient = a transfer of ownership.
• Despite owning it, the carrier answers only for negligence (CULPAM DUMTAXAT DEBERE).

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: employment (OPERARUM)
cards.front: LOCATIO CONDUCTIO OPERIS vs OPERARUM — how do Examples 63/64 (Lysippe and Nina) differ?
cards.back:
OPERIS owes a result (OPUS); OPERARUM owes services (OPERAE) over time under another's directions.
• Teaching one particular aria → OPERIS, done once Nina can sing it.
• Giving singing lessons → OPERARUM.
• Employee = LOCATOR renders services; employer = CONDUCTOR pays the wage.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: employment (OPERARUM)
cards.front: Who bears the wage risk in Roman employment contracts?
cards.back:
The employer owes the full wage if non-performance is not the employee's fault — decided by sphere.
• Employee's own illness → no wage.
• Employer's illness or death → borne by the employer side.
• Roman employment was marginal: most labour came from slaves.

cards.topic: Ch. VII — Locatio conductio: employment (OPERARUM)
cards.front: Ulpian D 19.2.19.9: scribe B is hired for a year at a fixed wage; employer A dies soon after. Wage for the whole year?
cards.back:
Yes — rescript of Caracalla and Septimius Severus: not the scribe's fault his services were not rendered.
• But minus what he earns from someone else that year.
• Modern parallel: § 1155 ABGB.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: What is MANDATUM?
cards.back:
A consensual contract by which the MANDATARIUS undertakes to carry out, free of charge, a legal or factual act for the MANDATOR.
• Rests on agreement — not a one-sided command, despite "to mandate" = "to order".
• Necessarily gratuitous: a "transaction among friends" (AMICITIA).
• BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM: the INTENTIO refers to OPORTERE EX FIDE BONA.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Why is MANDATUM an imperfectly bilateral contract, and which actions arise from it?
cards.back:
The MANDATOR always has a performance claim; the MANDATARIUS' counterclaims can, but need not, arise.
• ACTIO MANDATI DIRECTA: performance and surrender of what was obtained.
• ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA: MANDATARIUS claims expenses and losses.
• No remuneration — the mandate is necessarily gratuitous.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: What is RES INTEGRA, and how can a mandate be ended unilaterally?
cards.back:
RES INTEGRA = termination still causes neither side reliance loss; while it exists, either party may end the mandate.
• Agreement matters for formation and for continuation.
• Unilateral declaration: REVOCATIO (by the MANDATOR) or RENUNTIATIO (by the MANDATARIUS).
• Note: the book's print appears to swap these two labels.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: What kind of act can be the object of a mandate, and whose affair must it be?
cards.back:
A legal or a factual act, conducted for someone else — not solely in the MANDATARIUS' own interest.
• Legal act: standing surety for the MANDATOR.
• Factual act: erecting a statue in his honour.
• Common interest possible: a mandate only insofar as the MANDATOR's interest differs.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: MANDATUM vs CONSILIUM (MANDATUM TUA GRATIA) — what is the difference?
cards.back:
A "mandate" purely in the agent's own interest is non-binding advice (CONSILIUM), not MANDATUM (Gaius D 17.1.2.6, Case 174/1).
• Sources call it MANDATUM TUA GRATIA — misleading, technically no mandate.
• Adviser is not liable if things go wrong (Gai Inst 3.156, Case 173).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Case 175 (Ulpian/Celsus D 17.1.16): Aurelius Quietus has his physician build a ball court and baths in the physician's gardens at Ravenna, at Quietus' expense. Recoverable?
cards.back:
Only insofar as the costs exceed the increase in value of the physician's own property (ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA).
• The value increase served the physician's own interest.
• Only the excess was spent purely in the MANDATOR's interest.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Property link: indirect agency in mandate (Example 65) — how does the MANDATOR become owner?
cards.back:
The MANDATARIUS acquires first in his own name, then transfers to the MANDATOR by a second TRADITIO.
• Achilles buys from Drakon for Pomona and receives by TRADITIO himself.
• Classical law: SUI IURIS persons generally act only as indirect agents.
• Direct agency (immediate effect on the principal) was generally not available.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: What does the MANDATARIUS owe — main duty and secondary duties?
cards.back:
Carry out the transaction as agreed, safeguarding the MANDATOR's interests (e.g. hand over what he bought).
• Secondary duties from BONA FIDES: protection, care, information.
• Report impossibility promptly (Gaius D 17.1.27.2, Case 185).
• Report other important facts (Ulpian D 17.1.29.3, Case 177).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Example 66: seriously ill Laura asks Xerxes to bring a medicine from Greece; he breaks his leg. What must he do?
cards.back:
Tell her promptly so she can ask someone else; failing to inform = CULPA LATA → liable.
• Cf Gaius D 17.1.27.2 (Case 185).
• If Laura dies before he leaves, the contract lapses (MANDATUM MORTE SOLVITUR).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: What is the MANDATARIUS' standard of liability, and what may the MANDATOR claim?
cards.back:
As a rule only DOLUS and CULPA LATA — fitting a gratuitous act of friendship.
• Typical breach: not performing although he could have.
• Culpable non-performance → expectation interest (Gaius D 17.1.27.2, Case 185).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Which expenses must the MANDATOR reimburse? (Example 67)
cards.back:
Only those incurred BONA FIDE in duly performing the mandate (Gaius D 17.1.27.4, Case 178).
• Bellona, asked to deliver Agathon's message, hires a horse though riding was not agreed.
• Horse hire is outside the mandate → not reimbursed.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Example 68: Vibia buys a slave for Solon; while staying at her house the slave steals from her. Can she claim?
cards.back:
Yes — a loss directly linked to executing the mandate; ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA against Solon.
• Principal liable irrespective of fault ("liability for risk").
• Extent disputed: the slave's value only, or the whole loss?

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Slave bought under a mandate steals from the MANDATARIUS: limited or full liability of the MANDATOR? (Neratius/Paulus vs Julian)
cards.back:
Neratius and Paulus: limited to the slave's value, by analogy to noxal liability; Julian: the whole loss.
• Paulus (Neratius) D 17.1.26.7 (Case 182).
• Africanus (Julian) D 47.2.62(61).5 (Case 181).
• Clearly the whole loss if he knew the slave was a thief and did not warn.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Why does the MANDATOR bear the risk of accidental losses, and where is the limit? (Example 69)
cards.back:
Whoever benefits from a gratuitous performance carries the risk of accidental harm — but not the general risk of life.
• Orestes, robbed of 100 carrying Elektra's message → no claim.
• Robbery, shipwreck, illness are not mandate-specific (Paulus D 17.1.26.6, Case 179).
• Rationale: Africanus (Julian) D 47.2.62(61).5 last sentence (Case 181).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: concept and duties of the parties
cards.front: Example 70: Omphale asks Teukros to obtain a painting, then buys it herself. Any duty?
cards.back:
She must tell Teukros so he stops trying — the MANDATOR, too, has BONA FIDES secondary duties.
• Protection, care and information toward the MANDATARIUS.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: Impossibility without fault in a mandate — what are the consequences?
cards.back:
MANDATARIUS not liable; MANDATOR cannot demand performance but reimburses expenses incurred before the impossibility.
• The MANDATARIUS must notify the MANDATOR.
• Not obtainable at the agreed price, bought dearer: no delivery claim.
• Offer and acceptance at the higher price = a new contract.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: Case 183 (Gai Inst 3.161): E mandates T to buy land for 100,000 sesterces; T pays 150,000 though 100,000 would have sufficed. Position?
cards.back:
E has ACTIO MANDATI for his interest; he may, but need not, take the land — even at 100,000.
• T has no expense claim if E refuses.
• Gaius follows Sabinus and Cassius: T's culpable breach.
• Remarkable: T gets nothing even if willing to hand over at 100,000.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: Exceeding the mandate's price limit: Sabinian vs Proculian view?
cards.back:
Sabinians: the MANDATARIUS has no claim at all; Proculians: if he hands over the land, he recovers the agreed 100,000.
• Sabinian view: Gai Inst 3.161 (Case 183).
• Proculian view: Gaius D 17.1.4 (Case 184/2).
• Possible but not done as agreed → liable for the MANDATOR's interest.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: What does MANDATUM MORTE SOLVITUR mean, and what are its exceptions?
cards.back:
Death of either party ends the mandate — a highly personal relationship; rights and duties do not pass to heirs.
• Execution already begun: heir reimburses expenses; gains go to the heirs.
• MANDATARIUS acting BONA FIDE, unaware of the death: ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA (Gai Inst 3.160, Case 186).

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: What is the loan mandate (MANDATUM QUALIFICATUM)?
cards.back:
A mandates B to lend money to C in B's own name and at B's expense; A covers B's loss if C defaults.
• Functionally a guarantee (cf § 778 BGB).
• B cannot claim the sum lent as an "expense" — only his loss on default.
• Unlike the loan on order: the loan arises between MANDATARIUS and third party.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: Case 173 (Gai Inst 3.156): Ego urges Tu to lend out idle money at interest; the borrower defaults. Is Ego liable — and if he named Titius?
cards.back:
General urging: no — mere MANDATUM TUA GRATIA; naming Titius: a MANDATUM, Tu recovers by ACTIO MANDATI CONTRARIA.
• Tu must then lend to Titius.
• If Titius defaults, Tu recovers his loss from Ego.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: impossibility, death, loan mandate
cards.front: Urging someone to lend to a specific borrower: binding mandate or mere advice? (Sabinus/Gaius vs Servius)
cards.back:
Sabinus and Gaius: a binding MANDATUM; Servius reportedly saw even this as mere advice.
• Controversial in classical law (Gai Inst 3.156, Case 173).
• Lending generally at interest, no borrower named: advice for all.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: CESSIO, NOVATIO, IN REM SUAM
cards.front: What is CESSIO, and why was it hard to achieve in Roman law?
cards.back:
Transfer of a claim so that a new creditor (cessionary) instead of the cedent can demand performance from the debitor cessus.
• OBLIGATIO = a personal bond between creditor and debtor only.
• Change of creditor generally only via NOVATIO by stipulation, at the original creditor's request.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: CESSIO, NOVATIO, IN REM SUAM
cards.front: What is NOVATIO and what are its effects?
cards.back:
Replacement of an existing obligation by a new one, by stipulation; the old one is extinguished with its securities.
• Pledges and guarantees attached to the old claim fall away.
• Can change the creditor, the debtor or the legal ground.
• E.g. lessor's rent claim turned by stipulation into an obligation enforceable by CONDICTIO.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: CESSIO, NOVATIO, IN REM SUAM
cards.front: Example 71: Melitta owes Achilles 800, due in two years; Pytheas pays Achilles 700 for the claim. How does Pytheas get it?
cards.back:
At Achilles' request Melitta promises Pytheas by stipulation what she owes — NOVATIO; Achilles' claim is extinguished.
• Underlying deal: purchase of a not-yet-due claim for 700.
• Creditor directing his debtor to bind himself to a new creditor = DELEGATIO OBLIGANDI.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: CESSIO, NOVATIO, IN REM SUAM
cards.front: What is MANDATUM AD AGENDUM IN REM SUAM?
cards.back:
The creditor mandates the new creditor to sue the debtor; if he may keep the proceeds, it works like a cession.
• No consent of the debtor needed.
• IN REM SUAM: the MANDATARIUS litigates for himself and keeps the proceeds.
• Basis for keeping them may be a sale of the claim.

cards.topic: Ch. VIII — Mandatum: CESSIO, NOVATIO, IN REM SUAM
cards.front: What were the weaknesses of the MANDATUM IN REM SUAM, and how were they overcome?
cards.back:
Formally he still enforces another's claim: the debtor may pay the MANDATOR; death or revocation ends the mandate.
• MANDATOR-debtor deal on extension or waiver → EXCEPTIO against the MANDATARIUS.
• Rescripts: ACTIO UTILIS despite the MANDATOR's death (Gordianus C 4.10.1).
• Antoninus Pius: inheritance buyer's ACTIO UTILIS (Ulpian D 2.14.16 pr) → medieval CESSIO theory.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: concept, shares, liability
cards.front: What is SOCIETAS?
cards.back:
Two or more persons join to pursue a common economic purpose; consensual contract enforced by ACTIO PRO SOCIO (BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM).
• Not an exchange of performances but joint activity toward the agreed aim.
• Agreement defines the goal and contributions; the rest follows from BONA FIDES.
• No legal person — it governs only the partners' internal relations.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: concept, shares, liability
cards.front: How are profit and loss shares fixed in a SOCIETAS, and what is a SOCIETAS LEONINA?
cards.back:
By agreement; if unclear, equal shares. A SOCIETAS LEONINA — one partner only losses, another only profits — is void.
• Equal shares: Ulpian D 17.2.29 pr (Case 189).
• Larger profit with smaller loss share allowed (Gai Inst 3.149, Case 188).
• LEONINA offends AEQUITAS (Ulpian D 17.2.29.2, Case 189).
• Contributions may be in kind, capital or labour.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: concept, shares, liability
cards.front: What is the standard of liability between partners (DILIGENTIA QUAM IN SUIS REBUS)?
cards.back:
The care a partner usually shows in his own affairs — subjective CULPA IN CONCRETO, not the BONUS PATER FAMILIAS.
• Liability for DOLUS and CULPA; in special cases CUSTODIA.
• Rationale: whoever picks a careless partner has only himself to blame (Gaius D 17.2.72, Case 198).

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: concept, shares, liability
cards.front: What is the BENEFICIUM COMPETENTIAE in the ACTIO PRO SOCIO?
cards.back:
Privileged condemnation: the SOCIUS pays only ID QUOD FACERE POTEST — what he can afford.
• Exception: a partner who fraudulently reduced his means (Ulpian D 17.2.63 pr, Case 201).

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: concept, shares, liability
cards.front: Paulus D 17.2.25 (Case 197): may a partner offset a loss he negligently caused against a gain he made for the SOCIETAS elsewhere?
cards.back:
No — COMPENSATIO LUCRI CUM DAMNO (deducting gains from damages) is rejected here.
• The concept fits where the harmful event itself also benefits the injured party.
• Modern tort law: "set-off of benefits".

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: Case 200 (Ulpian/Julian D 17.2.52.4): partner A in the clothing trade is robbed on a buying trip. Who bears the loss?
cards.back:
Shared: Julian gives A the ACTIO PRO SOCIO against partner B for half.
• Covers the money and goods A carried for purchasing.
• Test: pursuing the business purpose was CONDICIO SINE QUA NON of the loss.
• Contrast mandate: robbery is general risk of life (Case 179).

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: Case 196 (Ulpian/Celsus D 17.2.58 pr): T (three horses) and E (one) agree to sell them as a quadriga; E's horse dies before the sale. Who bears it?
cards.back:
E alone: the purpose was only selling; it became impossible, the partnership dissolved, and E gets no share of T's sale.
• If they intended to co-own the QUADRIGA: loss shared according to shares.
• Shared risk covers risks typical of the agreed business purpose.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: On which grounds does a SOCIETAS end?
cards.back:
Termination (RENUNTIATIO) plus four further grounds.
• A partner's death or insolvency.
• Aim achieved.
• Purpose becomes impossible.
• Expiry of the agreed term (fixed-term partnership).

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: RENUNTIATIO of a SOCIETAS — what are its limits?
cards.back:
Any partner may renounce, dissolving the whole SOCIETAS — but not untimely, and a fixed-term one only for important reasons.
• Untimely = losses a later reasonable date would avoid → compensate (Ulpian D 17.2.14, Case 194).
• Important reasons: essential condition fails, or a partner's damage makes continuing unreasonable.
• RENUNTIATIO EX NECESSITATE (Paulus D 17.2.65.6, Case 193).

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: Contribution QUOAD USUM vs QUOAD SORTEM vs QUOAD DOMINIUM — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Three ways of contributing a thing: only its use, its value internally, or co-ownership.
• USUM: contributor keeps ownership, contributes the use only.
• SORTEM: owner toward third parties; internally partnership property, divided on dissolution.
• DOMINIUM: co-ownership (CONDOMINIUM) of all partners in agreed shares.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: Property link: SOCIETAS vs co-ownership — can the partnership itself own its assets?
cards.back:
No — SOCIETAS lacks legal personality; assets belong to single partners or jointly (CONDOMINIUM) to several or all.
• CONDOMINIUM: each co-owner holds an ideal quota and may dispose of it.
• SOCIETAS is a contract (obligations); co-ownership is property law — they may coexist.
• Dissolution: ACTIO PRO SOCIO for accounts, ACTIO COMMUNI DIVIDUNDO for co-owned things.

cards.topic: Ch. IX — Societas: risk, end, partnership assets
cards.front: Examples 72/73: restaurants run as partnerships — when is ACTIO PRO SOCIO enough, and when is ACTIO COMMUNI DIVIDUNDO needed?
cards.back:
Agatha (premises) and Midas (labour): only ACTIO PRO SOCIO; Kreon and Hecuba's jointly bought land: also ACTIO COMMUNI DIVIDUNDO.
• Agatha keeps ownership — no change in property law.
• ACTIO PRO SOCIO: settlement of accounts, profit and loss shares.
• Joint acquisition within the partnership creates co-ownership.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: What are innominate contracts?
cards.back:
Actionable agreements whose content fits none of the recognised contract types.
• No standard action available (ACTIO CERTAE CREDITAE PECUNIAE, ACTIO EMPTI, ACTIO LOCATI etc.).
• Requires synallagmatically linked performances.
• Classically enforced by ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: What are the four patterns of innominate contracts?
cards.back:
DO UT DES, DO UT FACIAS, FACIO UT FACIAS, FACIO UT DES — combinations of DARE and FACERE.
• Each performance is promised in order to get the other (SYNALLAGMA).
• Exchange (PERMUTATIO) = DO UT DES.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Which two prerequisites must be met to claim performance under an innominate contract?
cards.back:
A synallagmatic link of the performances and — commonly named — prior performance by the claimant, at least in part.
• Hence the name "innominate real contracts".
• Contrast EMPTIO VENDITIO and LOCATIO CONDUCTIO: claims arise on mere consensus.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Case 208a (Ulpian/Julian D 19.5.13.1): E transfers land to T, who is to build a house on part of it and transfer that part back. Which contract?
cards.back:
An innominate contract — Julian rejects sale, mandate and partnership.
• No sale: no fixed money price.
• No mandate: a remuneration was agreed.
• No partnership: focus on the SYNALLAGMA, not a shared business aim.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Case 204 (Ulpian D 19.5.17.3): E and T lend each other their oxen for ten days each; one ox dies. Which action, which standard?
cards.back:
ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS — innominate contract, not COMMODATUM, since use is exchanged for use.
• Liability by analogy: negligence up to CUSTODIA.
• Same standard as in COMMODATUM and LOCATIO CONDUCTIO REI.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Case 210a (Pomponius D 19.5.16.1): T lets E sow on T's land, then refuses to let him harvest. Remedy?
cards.back:
Only damages via ACTIO DE DOLO, the subsidiary delictual remedy.
• No recognised contract type.
• No innominate contract either: no SYNALLAGMA — E owed no counter-performance.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: CONDICTIO CAUSA DATA CAUSA NON SECUTA vs ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS — what does each achieve?
cards.back:
CONDICTIO (earlier law): restitution of one's own performance; ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS (classical): enforcement of the counter-performance.
• CONDICTIO = OB CAUSAM DATORUM = OB REM — unjust enrichment.
• ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS: a BONAE FIDEI IUDICIUM.
• Normally available only once the claimant has performed.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Case 205 (Papinian D 19.5.7): E gives T ten gold coins so that T frees the slave Stichus; T does not. E's actions?
cards.back:
ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS for his interest in the manumission, or CONDICTIO (OB CAUSAM DATORUM) for the coins.
• Pattern: DO UT FACIAS.
• Choice: expectation interest vs restitution.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: concept and enforcement
cards.front: Why is it called ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS, and what other names does it have?
cards.back:
The formula is preceded by a description of the specific agreement (DEMONSTRATIO); the INTENTIO frames a IUS CIVILE claim.
• ACTIO INCERTI CIVILIS (Ulpian/Maurician D 2.14.7.2, Case 202).
• ACTIO IN FACTUM CIVILIS (Ulpian D 19.5.13 pr, Case 208).
• Not the praetorian ACTIO IN FACTUM CONCEPTA (Julian in D 2.14.7.2).

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: PERMUTATIO (exchange): sale or innominate contract? (Sabinians vs Proculians)
cards.back:
The Proculian view prevailed: a money price is essential to EMPTIO VENDITIO, so exchange is an innominate contract.
• Sabinians first treated barter as sale (Paulus D 18.1.1.1, Case 52).
• ABGB: exchange (§§ 1045 ff) and sale (§§ 1053 ff) partly identical rules.
• § 480 BGB applies sale rules analogously.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: Exchange vs sale — what must the party perform, and when does a claim arise?
cards.back:
Exchange (DO UT DES): claim arises from DARE — making the other owner; sale: consensus suffices, seller owes undisturbed possession.
• Handing over another's thing creates no exchange claim (Pedius in Paulus D 19.4.1.3).

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: What is the aestimatory contract (AESTIMATUM)?
cards.back:
E hands T goods to sell; if sold, T pays the estimated value and keeps any surplus; unsold, T returns them.
• Unsold goods are returned after a set period.
• Enforced by ACTIO DE AESTIMATO, an ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS.
• The edict apparently had a model formula (Ulpian D 19.3.1, Case 207).

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: Case 208 (Ulpian D 19.5.13 pr): E gives T an item to sell at a fixed price; T may keep any surplus. Why no mandate, SOCIETAS, sale or lease?
cards.back:
An innominate contract: T is not gratuitous, has no partnership intent, may return unsold goods, and his reward is not fixed.
• Mandate: T would sell gratuitously and hand over all proceeds.
• SOCIETAS: the giver gets a fixed price, not a share.
• Sale/lease: return possible; reward depends on whether and at what price he sells.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: Aestimatum as SOCIETAS (Ulpian D 17.2.44, Case 195) — why is that classification doubtful?
cards.back:
Ulpian: SOCIETAS if they intend a partnership to sell — one contributes goods, the other selling effort; a common purpose is doubtful.
• The giver wants the estimated value.
• The dealer wants to sell above it and keep the surplus.
• Without partnership intent: innominate contract (Case 208).

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: How are duties, liability and risk determined in innominate contracts?
cards.back:
By the agreement (ID QUOD ACTUM EST) and by analogy to the most similar nominate contract; liability follows the utility principle.
• Scope, defective performance, liability and risk: as in the closest nominate contract.
• Modern parallel: atypical or mixed contracts handled by analogy to regulated types.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: CONTRACTUS MOHATRAE (Ulpian/Labeo D 19.5.19 pr, Case 210) and AESTIMATUM: the goods perish before the sale — who bears the loss?
cards.back:
Whoever had the main interest: in MOHATRAE usually the recipient (his borrowing interest) — liable for all fault and all accidents.
• Giver's interest predominates → recipient liable only for culpable loss.
• AESTIMATUM: same test; seller always liable for DOLUS and CULPA (Ulpian D 19.5.17.1, Case 209).
• MOHATRAE: MUTUUM arises only when the recipient receives the price.

cards.topic: Ch. X — Innominate contracts: exchange, aestimatum, liability
cards.front: Case 206 (Ulpian D 19.5.20 pr): E lets T test horses for three days; T wins a trick-riding competition on them, then declines to buy. E's remedy?
cards.back:
ACTIO PRAESCRIPTIS VERBIS: the agreement allowed testing, not competing — presumably for the prize money.
• Subsidiary function: surrender of a gain from conduct outside the agreement, not counter-performance.
• No CONDICTIO: the gain does not stem from a payment E made to T.
